PRACTICAL PEARL
Acute Respiratory Failure in a Patient with Stiff-Person
Syndrome
Vincent Jachiet 1 • Laurent Laine 1 • Thierry Gendre 2 • Carole Henry 2 •
Daniel Da Silva 1 • Etienne de Montmollin 1
Published online: 18 July 2016
/C211Springer Science+Business Media New York 2016
Abstract
Background Stiff-person syndrome (SPS) is a rare disorder
characterized by progressive muscle stiffness, rigidity, and
spasms involving the axial muscles. Acute respiratory
distress has rarely been reported in this condition.
Methods We report a case of a 49-year-old woman with
autoimmune SPS diagnosed during an episode of acute
respiratory failure secondary to repetitive episodes of
apnea, requiring intensive care.
Results Acute respiratory failure manifesting with apneic
episodes is a life-threatening and unpredictable complica-
tion of SPS. Its pathophysiology is not well known. The
two suggested mechanisms are as follows: (1) apnea due to
muscle rigidity and paroxysmal muscle spasms, and (2)
paroxysmal autonomic hyperactivity. Sudden and unex-
pected deaths have been reported in SPS, and all described
cases have been associated with apnea. Thus, the onset of
apnea during SPS should be considered a criterion of high
severity and should lead to intensive care unit (ICU)
admission for continuous monitoring. In patients with
severe disease who are unresponsive to symptomatic
treatment with benzodiazepines and baclofen, or in patients
with life-threatening complications, early immunotherapy
by intravenous immunoglobulins should be considered.
Conclusion Onset of apneas during SPS should be con-
sidered as a signal of possible progression toward acute
respiratory failure and sudden death, and should lead to
ICU admission for continuous monitoring. Early
immunotherapy should be started in such situations,
including intravenous immunoglobulins as the ﬁrst-line
treatment.

Acute respiratory failure /C1Apnea /C1
Intravenous immunoglobulins
Introduction
Stiff-person spectrum disorder (SPSD) is a rare disease
characterized by progressive muscle stiffness, rigidity, and
spasms involving the axial muscles and results in severely
impaired ambulation [1]. SPSD has an estimated prevalence
of one to two cases per million, with an incidence of one
case per million per year [ 2]. Apart from classic stiff-person
syndrome (SPS), clinical presentations include stiff-limb
syndrome (SLS) and progressive encephalomyelitis with
rigidity and myoclonus. There can also be overlaps between
SPSD and ataxic, epileptic and encephalitic syndromes [ 3].
There is an important phenotypical variability of SPSD,
with several associated autoantibodies; and a classiﬁcation
based on likely etiology has been proposed [ 4]. Autoim-
mune SPS (70 %) is deﬁned by the autoantibody positivity
in the absence of underlying malignancy. It is often asso-
ciated with type 1 diabetes mellitus, thyroiditis, vitiligo,
and pernicious anemia. Anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase
(GAD) antibodies are the most common antibodies, with
high titers and anti-GAD65 speciﬁcity, followed by anti-
glycine receptor (GlyR) antibodies. Paraneoplastic SPS
(20 %) is deﬁned by all cases emerging in the context of
cancer. Associated malignancies include breast and lung
cancers and Hodgkin lymphoma. Anti-GAD65 and anti-

GlyR are less frequently found, and anti-amphiphysin
antibodies can also be detected. Cryptogenic SPS (10 %) is
deﬁned by seronegative cases in which an immunologic
cause cannot be identiﬁed.
The diagnosis is often delayed due to the rarity of the
disease and the lack of knowledge of this condition by
clinicians. In severe cases of SPSD, apnea and sudden
death have been described [ 5–7]. The link between both
phenomena is still a matter of debate. We report a case of
SPS diagnosed during an episode of acute respiratory
failure, requiring intensive care.
Case Presentation
A 49-year-old woman was admitted to our intensive care
unit (ICU) from the emergency room because of hypox-
emic acute respiratory failure secondary to repetitive
episodes of apnea concomitant to spasms of her axial
muscles. She had a history of type 1 diabetes mellitus,
obesity, hyperthyroidism, and pernicious anemia. On
questioning, the patient had been experiencing gradual
onset of stiffness, rigidity, and pain in her axial muscles for
9 years, eventually leading to the inability to assume a
sitting posture. She also reported episodic muscle spasms
of the limbs that were triggered by sound stimulation. The
persistent nature of her symptoms led to pronounced
lumbar lordosis. Functional consequences were pro-
nounced with repeated falls, fractures, and loss of
autonomy. During the past 6 months, she developed more
frequent self-limiting acute episodes of dyspnea with cya-
nosis, lasting between 5 and 45 min, associated with
hypertonic stiffness of axial muscles.
Clinical examination during hypertonic crisis showed
low-grade fever, tachycardia, arterial hypertension, profuse
sweating, agitation, apnea, cyanosis, and an oxygen satu-
ration level as low as 60 %. Neurologic examination was
normal between hypertonic crises; and there was no sign of
encephalitis, myoclonus, or ataxia. Auscultation and chest
x-ray revealed no sign of aspiration pneumonia. Laboratory
tests revealed neutrophilic leukocytosis with normal C-re-
active protein, elevated serum creatine phosphokinase less
than double the standard, and normal renal and hepatic
functions.
Because oxygen saturation failed to return to normal
between spasm episodes, she underwent orotracheal intu-
bation and mechanical ventilation. Diagnosis of SPS was
suggested on clinical presentation and conﬁrmed by an
electromyographic study revealing continuous motor-unit
activity and the presence of high titer of circulating anti-
GAD antibodies ( >1500 U/mL, N < 1 U/mL), with anti-
GAD65 (79 U, N < 5) speciﬁcity. Cranial magnetic res-
onance imaging, electroencephalography, and analysis of
cerebrospinal ﬂuid were normal. She was immunized
against tetanus.
Symptomatic treatment was initiated with benzodi-
azepine (midazolam 10 mg/h continuous intravenous
infusion) and baclofen. Despite adequate sedation, man-
agement of airway pressures was difﬁcult due to persistent
episodes of axial muscle stiffness and required the use of
neuromuscular blocking agents. The patient was not,
however, hypoxemic and was ventilated in assist-control
mode with an inspired oxygen fraction of 30 %. Symp-
tomatic treatment was intensiﬁed with a high dose of
diazepam (10 mg/h continuous infusion), and intravenous
immunoglobulins (IVIG) (2 g/kg over 5 days) were started
3 days after admission. Following IVIG therapy, we
observed a rapid clinical improvement with the disap-
pearance of muscle stiffness and apnea, allowing the

reduction of diazepam doses. The patient was weaned off
from mechanical ventilation at 10 days after ICU admis-
sion. There was no hemodynamic or renal failure during
the ICU stay. IVIG treatment continued every 6 weeks
with persistent clinical improvement. Five months after
ICU discharge, the patient relapsed without apnea but with
severe functional impairment, and immunotherapy was
intensiﬁed to include rituximab.
Discussion
Acute respiratory failure manifesting with apneic episodes
is a life-threatening and unpredictable complication of
SPSD. Its pathophysiology is unclear, and the two sug-
gested mechanisms are as follows: (1) apnea due to muscle
rigidity and paroxysmal muscle spasms, and (2) paroxys-
mal autonomic hyperactivity. Both these conditions may
result from the same autoimmune pathogenic mechanism
directed against GABAergic neurons [ 5]. It is thought that
impairment of GABAergic pathways by autoantibodies and
a reduction of brain GABA result in clinical manifestations
of stiffness, spasms, and phobias [ 2]. Thus, respiratory
difﬁculties may be caused by spasms of the diaphragm,
impaired respiratory function, and sudden tonic rigidity
involving the respiratory muscles [ 6]. The lack of
GABAergic inhibition in the intermediolateral cell column,
however, may lead to sympathetic overactivity [ 8]. This
autonomic hyperactivity can lead to paroxysmal attacks of
transient arterial hypertension, hyperpyrexia, tachycardia,
pupillary dilatation, agitation, and diaphoresis during
painful muscle spasms. In our case, mechanical ventilation
by itself did not alleviate respiratory symptoms; and only
neuromuscular blocking agents allowed correct ventilation
parameters, advocating for the ﬁrst mechanism. Sudden
and unexpected deaths have been reported in SPSD, and all
described cases have been associated with apnea [ 5–7].

Thus, we believe that the onset of apnea during SPSD,
regardless of the underlying mechanism, should be con-
sidered as a criterion of high severity and should lead to
ICU admission for continuous monitoring until the effect
of immunotherapy.
In patients with severe disease who are unresponsive to
symptomatic treatment with benzodiazepines and baclofen,
or in patients with life-threatening complications, early
immunotherapy by IVIG should be considered [ 9]. The
rapid onset of IVIG therapy acts in favor of its use in the
context of life-threatening complications [ 10]. Rituximab
has also been used with success in SPSD refractory to IVIG
[11].
Conclusion
Onset of apnea during SPSD should be considered as a
signal of possible progression toward acute respiratory
failure and sudden death and should lead to ICU admission
for continuous monitoring. Early immunotherapy should be
started in such situations, including IVIG as the ﬁrst-line
treatment.
